summary: Gives more detail on how policy fits into the Path Computation Element architecture, and proposes using the Policy Core Information Model as a framework for path computation policy. It includes example scenarios. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: Network operators may need routes to follow rules about cost, service, or network boundaries. RFC 5394 describes where policy decisions can be applied when a network computes paths.

questions: how to control path computation decisions
what is a policy decision point
how can policies affect a pce route
subtitle: A framework for applying operator policies to path-computation requests and decisions

tldr.problem: Path computation needs to reflect service, client, and provider rules that are not captured by a single route algorithm.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5394 describes policy components around Path Computation Clients and Elements and introduces the Policy Core Information Model as a framework.
tldr.outcome: The document provides architecture and scenarios, not specific policies or a protocol. It leaves path-computation policy model details to separate work.

today: RFC 5394 is an Informational framework published in December 2008. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it describes architecture rather than defining specific policies.

sections.title: Why Path Computation Needs Policy
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) calculates routes for a Path Computation Client (PCC). Operators may want different constraints or optimization goals for different services, such as minimizing delay for one service and cost for another.

RFC 5394 describes using policy rules to guide those requests and decisions. Its goal is to let operators introduce path-computation behavior without requiring changes to the PCC-PCE communication protocol for every new constraint.
sections.plainLanguage: Different services can need different routes. Policy lets operators express those differences as rules for path computation.

sections.title: Examples of Path Policies
sections.content:
The RFC gives examples such as choosing a preconfigured path for a service, selecting a transit provider, or applying different constraints to different service types. A policy may also relax a constraint and retry when a path cannot be found.

For load balancing, policies may use offered traffic load to direct requests to different exits. This can use information that is not represented as a traffic-engineering link or node attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: A policy can prefer a particular provider, apply service-specific route requirements, or distribute traffic using measured load.

sections.title: Policy Repositories and Decision Points
sections.content:
The framework uses a Policy Core Information Model (PCIM) as a way to represent policy rules. It describes policy repositories and two logical functions: a Policy Decision Point retrieves applicable policies, and a Policy Enforcement Point applies them to the PCC or PCE's work.

Policy can be applied at a PCC, at a PCE, or at both. The PCC may select a PCE and shape a request; the PCE may validate it, choose constraints or algorithms, and decide whether to compute locally or ask another PCE.
sections.plainLanguage: A repository stores policy rules. Decision and enforcement functions use those rules at the client, the path-computation element, or both.

sections.title: Requests, Responses, and New Constraints
sections.content:
A path-computation request can carry policy information that describes a service and its requirements. The PCE applies request-specific and local policies, then may compute a path, ask another PCE for help, reject the request, or return information about which constraints were honored or relaxed.

The framework aims to let a PCE add a new constraint with limited changes. Policy-aware components can use it, while PCCs and PCEs that do not process it need not be modified. The RFC does not define the specific policy behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The PCE uses policies to decide how to handle a request and can report which requirements it met. A new policy can be added without changing every network component.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The framework adds security concerns around policy repositories and policy information carried in requests and responses. Threats include unauthorized access, interception, impersonation, falsified policy data, and denial of service.

The RFC expects PCE solutions to address these issues in detail. It does not define a single security protocol for the framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers who change or impersonate policy information could influence route decisions. Implementations need to protect policy stores and communications.
